The fourfinger threadfin, Eleutheronema tetradactylum, is a large-bodied polynemid found in coastal and estuarine waters across the Indo-West Pacific. This species exhibits an impressive asymptotic size, with the largest individuals reaching a total length of 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters]. Such substantial ultimate dimensions are characteristic of the genus and reflect the species' position as a high-order predator within its inshore and brackish habitats. Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency analysis indicate that males and females grow at comparable rates during the early years of life, though females tend to achieve slightly greater maximum sizes. The species' rapid early growth is fuelled by a diet dominated by penaeid prawns, small teleosts, and occasionally polychaetes, a feeding ecology that also makes it highly vulnerable to commercial trawl fisheries throughout its range.

Reproductive biology in Eleutheronema tetradactylum is closely tied to the monsoon-driven productivity cycles of tropical estuaries. Sexual maturation is attained at a relatively modest size, with the total length at puberty measuring 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds approximately to the end of the second year of life in most populations, though local variation depending on resource availability has been documented. The onset of gonadal recrudescence is signalled by an increase in the gonadosomatic index during the pre-monsoon period, with peak spawning activity coinciding with elevated rainfall and riverine discharge. Larger, older females contribute disproportionately to reproductive output, as fecundity scales strongly with body size and weight in this polynemid species.

At a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], which is representative of typical monsoon-season conditions in tropical nursery grounds, the species attains a maximum lifespan of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. Longevity in this species is moderate for a polymixiid of its size, and field records of tagged individuals suggest that mortality rates increase sharply after the eighth year, particularly among heavily exploited populations where fishing pressure truncates the age structure. The same thermal regime is relevant to understanding the species' reproductive physiology. Under these stable warm conditions (28 °C), the daily reproductive rate is expressed through a combination of batch spawning events and high fecundity; females produce an average of approximately 137,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 137,000 eggs per spawning event] and can spawn multiple times across the protracted monsoon season, with an estimated frequency of about once every 10 days [F_R_i = multiple times across the protracted monsoon season, with an estimated frequency of about once every 10 days].

Early life history in Eleutheronema tetradactylum begins with the spawning of pelagic, transparent eggs that are approximately 0.775 millimeters in diameter. From this egg size, the wet weight at birth of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva is calculated to be around 0.00024 grams [Wwb = around 0.00024 grams]. This minute initial mass is typical of polynemid fishes that produce large numbers of small offspring as a bet-hedging strategy against high larval mortality in the plankton, a pattern consistent with other members of the Polydactylus genus. The lecithotrophic phase lasts only a few days, during which the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves. Following yolk-sac resorption, the onset of exogenous feeding begins when the mouth opens and retinal differentiation allows the larva to detect and capture small zooplankton, primarily copepod nauplii, in the turbid coastal waters that serve as the primary nursery habitat.

The ultimate weight attained by mature adults in Eleutheronema tetradactylum provides a striking contrast to their infinitesimally small beginnings. Large, fully grown individuals can reach an asymptotic body mass of up to 145,000 grams [Wwi = up to 145,000 grams], a value that underscores the extraordinary scope for somatic growth embedded in this species' life history. This maximum recorded wet weight is typically observed in older females from lightly exploited populations where individuals have been able to realise their full growth potential. The dramatic size disparity between the 0.00024 gram neonate and the 145,000 gram adult represents a weight increase spanning nearly nine orders of magnitude, a growth trajectory sustained by efficient food conversion and the occupation of a high-quality foraging niche within productive estuarine ecosystems.
